newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Drug firms worried as S.Africa govt relations sour.
newsitem.headline: Drug firms worried as S.Africa govt relations sour.

text.p: A war of words between the pharmaceuticals industry and the South African government may cause multinational firms to cut their operations in the country, a top industry figure warned on Monday.
Knut Seifert, chief executive of German drug giant Boehringer Mannheim's South African unit, said recent verbal attacks could make international pharmaceutical firms feel unwanted in South Africa.
"If an industry is not welcome in a country, then companies have to think about down-sizing of operations and moving into a more friendly environment," Seifert said in a statement.
Seifert was referring to accusations that the industry charged high prices for its medicines. He defended the sector and said the average unit price in South Africa was below European levels.
But Seifert's remarks will add further fire to a debate already raging about the role of the industry in South Africa.
They come hot on the heels of President Nelson Mandela's comments that the local industry is in the grip of multi-national firms trying to undermine Health Minister Nkosazana Zuma.

Mandela said her efforts to challenge multinationals' grip on the market had frightened some firms. In a thinly disguised reference to the drugs industry, he added that "white business" interests had played a role in a funding scandal over the Sarafina 2 AIDS play that has prompted calls for Zuma to quit.

Mirryena Deeb, chief executive of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association, said drugs firms played no part in the Sarafina scandal. "They (the government) seem to be linking our unhappiness with their own difficulties," she said.
The industry also denies it is a monopoly and says there are more than 200 players in the market.

Multinationals, such as Roche Holding ROCZg.Z and Glaxo Wellcome, do cover about 70 percent of the 4.5 billion rand sector, but local firms are strongly represented. South African Druggists, part of Malbak, is the biggest firm in the sector with 10.3 percent of the market.
"It is a highly competitive environment. To accuse us of being a monopoly is garbage. It is unfortunate the President has been fed inaccurate information," Deeb said.

Analysts say the debates over Sarafina and monopolies disguise more serious disputes. "The Sarafina debate is a storm in a tea-cup, but it is a sign of deeper problems," said one analyst who declined to be identified.

Zuma wants to make the prescription of generic drugs, which are cheaper versions of off-patent brands, mandatory for South African doctors. This has worried an industry which bases much of its riches on pushing brands and fiercely defending patents.
Deeb said the industry accepted the need for more use of cheaper generics, but said to make such a move mandatory hit at free competition and denied doctors and patients choice.
Zuma also wants to push through a marking system that will monitor where drugs end up and hit at the theft of medicines.

The industry expresses concern about crime, but estimates the 500 million rand a year cost of the scheme is too high. Deeb also said the problem occurred mostly in state depots that would be unaffected by firms marking their packaging.
The industry says good relations are vital for both sides.

Seifert, who was speaking as Boehringer global chief executive Gerald Moeller visited South Africa to open a new seven million rand office building, said drugs firms played a vital role in South Africa's developing economy.
"One should keep in mind that the pharmaceutical industry employs a lot of people, including mainly high skilled employees," he said.
